content: The resource pack on reducing human exposure to animal influenza viruses provides detailed information on this topic. It emphasizes the importance of thoroughly cooking all poultry-derived foods, including eggs and poultry blood. Cooked egg yolks should not be runny or liquid. Influenza viruses are destroyed by heat, so poultry meat should be cooked to an internal temperature of 70°C (158°F) in all parts, ensuring no pink meat remains. Proper handling and storage of meat are critical. Influenza viruses can be transmitted through the handling and slaughtering of live infected poultry. Good hygiene practices during slaughtering, de-feathering, and post-slaughter handling are essential to prevent direct exposure or cross-contamination with other foods, food preparation surfaces, or equipment. Refrigeration or freezing does not kill some influenza A viruses present in poultry meat. Meat by-products and food waste should be disposed of properly. Traditional food markets where live animals are present can facilitate the spread of influenza viruses between animals and from animals to humans. Best practices for market management include segregating animal trade activities from food market activities, ensuring trade involves only healthy animals as per official animal health authority guidelines, and promoting hygienic handling of animals, carcasses, and related products. Market zoning should be applied to avoid mixing animal species in the same area or mixing live animals with food products or slaughtering areas. Specific slaughtering areas should be defined, and primary processing of animals, especially poultry, should be centralized in authorized slaughterhouses. Safe and hygienic slaughter conditions should be ensured, and by-products should be disposed of properly. Areas for selling and slaughtering live animals should be separated from those open to the public. Contact between customers and live animals should be minimized, and customers should avoid touching animals and then touching their eyes, nose, or mouth. Markets should be cleaned daily, with proper waste disposal. A rest day should be organized at least twice a month for thorough cleaning and disinfection of all market areas, equipment, and utensils. Animals should not remain in the market on rest days. Market staff should be trained in good hygiene practices, including regular handwashing with soap and running water after handling animals and animal products. Producers should implement good animal production practices to reduce the risk of emergence and spread of avian influenza viruses. Drinking water from open surface water sources should be carefully treated to minimize risks to humans and animals. Properly treated wastewater poses minimal risk to humans, but recreational water might be contaminated in some cases. Feces from infected animals can be infectious, and dead animals should be buried appropriately. Influenza viruses can persist in water and wet surfaces for extended periods. Potential water reservoirs, especially in high-density animal production areas, should be identified and registered. Appropriate water treatment is strongly recommended for open water reservoirs used for drinking water supplies. If no community drinking water treatment system exists, the public should be advised to treat drinking water at the household level through boiling or chlorination. Wastewater treatment generally reduces virus concentrations but does not completely eliminate them. Open water contaminated with waterfowl feces may pose risks for bathing or swimming. Authorities should advise the public of potential risks and restrict access to contaminated sites if necessary. Infected birds can shed large amounts of influenza virus in their feces, and people should reduce contact with animal feces or take precautions as described in the resource pack. Dead infected animals and potentially contaminated solid waste should be disposed of appropriately by trained personnel following local regulations. Monitoring the health of individuals exposed to animals with influenza or to other people with zoonotic influenza is essential. Surveillance for zoonotic influenza should be increased, and coordination between animal health and public health sectors is critical during responses to zoonotic influenza cases. Suspected human cases of zoonotic influenza must be investigated to provide appropriate treatment, identify other potential human contacts, and determine if human-to-human transmission is occurring. Health care staff should be informed about the signs and symptoms of zoonotic influenza, how to explore patients’ exposure and travel histories, and how to report suspected cases. Enhanced surveillance is necessary when there has been human exposure to known outbreaks of influenza A viruses in animals or when a human case of infection is identified. Enhanced surveillance should include active screening in hospitals, inclusion of traditional healers and private practitioners, and monitoring of high-risk occupational groups such as health workers and those exposed to live or dead animals. Individuals exposed to animal influenza viruses or contacts of confirmed human cases should monitor their health for the duration of the exposure period plus an additional seven days. Testing of asymptomatic exposed individuals may be considered on a case-by-case basis. Specimen collection from suspected human cases is essential for virus identification, typing, and subtyping. Preferred specimens include upper respiratory tract samples, lower respiratory tract samples (if intubated), and blood for serum collection. Laboratories must be capable of processing and confirming human infections with animal influenza viruses. Virus sharing with WHO Collaborating Centres is vital for monitoring virus evolution, updating diagnostics and vaccines, and conducting risk assessments. WHO can assist with the shipping of samples to reference laboratories.
